articles.body: Nakodo's business campaigns look for local businesses to partner with, which means a customer draws a circle: this town, within 20km, or this whole country. Somewhere under that is a dataset of places that has to be loaded into our database before anything can search it. Loading "a circle" is not a thing you want to do twice. Two customers both looking around Manchester should cost one import, and a customer who widens from 15km to 25km should not re-import the middle. So the circle is not the unit of work. Grid cells are: const CELL = 0.5 ; // degrees const cellKey = ( lat0 : number , lng0 : number ) => `cell: ${ lat0 } , ${ lng0 } ` ; Half a degree is about 55km north to south, and the keys are shared by every campaign in the product.

articles.body: On 3 October I published a post here called Our daily API cap is three times last week's busiest day, because a fixed cap is a growth ceiling . The argument was that a constant daily cap on an outside source is a ceiling on your own growth, so the cap should follow recent use: today's limit is a multiple of the busiest of the last seven days, with a floor. On 10 October I deleted the whole mechanism. The type, the function, the lookback constant, the extra query, all of it. The argument in that post was not wrong about constants. It was wrong about the thing one level up, which is whether a limit shared by every account should exist at all. What the guard actually did when it fired Here is the deleted code: // Spike guards: caps that follow recent use instead of a fixed number.

articles.title: $667 or $1,100 for the same 100,000 JSON extractions — and the price per token never changed
articles.excerpt: Ask what an LLM call costs and you get the price list. Ask what a task costs and the honest answer is the price list divided by how often the answer is usable. That divisor is set by two knobs most be…
articles.body: Ask what an LLM call costs and you get the price list. Ask what a task costs and the honest answer is the price list divided by how often the answer is usable. That divisor is set by two knobs most beginners copy from a tutorial and never touch again — temperature and seed. A few words first. A token is roughly ¾ of a word; APIs bill per million of them, one price for input (what you send) and a higher one for output (what the model writes). Temperature controls how adventurous the model is when picking the next token: 0 means "almost always take the most likely one", 1 and above means "spread the bets". Seed is a number that makes that random choice repeatable — same seed, same input, (usually) same answer.

articles.excerpt: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, bringing a spectacular display of shooting stars to the autumn sky.
articles.body: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, triggering a spectacular display of shooting stars as Earth plunges through the densest part of the debris trail shed by Halley's Comet. Here's what you need to know. When is the best time to see Orionid shooting stars? Orionid meteors are best spotted between the hours of midnight and dawn on Oct. 22, when 10-20 shooting stars may be seen brightening the night sky each hour under ideal dark-sky. The glare cast by the 74%-lit waxing gibbous moon will hide fainter shooting stars for much of the night. Thankfully, the lunar disk will set a few hours after midnight, leaving a window of beautifully dark sky before dawn in which to enjoy the full majesty of the annual meteor shower.

An orbital view reveals the immense beauty of our blue planet, the only world we know of that hosts life. But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA. "You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere , and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission .

articles.body: I used to think being interested in the night sky meant I had to try every meteor shower. If a calendar said "peak," I interpreted that as an instruction. I'd set an alarm, find several layers of clothing and go outside at around 2:00 a.m. when even the neighborhood cats seemed surprised to see me. Then I'd spend an increasingly resentful 45 minutes staring upward, occasionally see one meteor and wonder whether I was somehow doing it all wrong. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective. The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet , which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside.

articles.title: Scientists find 'gemstones' in atmosphere of bizarre, scorching-hot 'marshmallow' exoplanet
articles.excerpt: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have unravelled some of the secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot exoplanet that has the consistency of marshmallow.
articles.body: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST , is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this " hot Jupiter " skyrocket.

articles.title: How to see the Orionid meteor shower 2026 peak this week — and when to look
articles.excerpt: The Orionids peak around Oct. 21. Here's when and where to look for the best chance of spotting meteors.
articles.body: If you love watching meteors, 2026 has given you plenty to enjoy. This summer, the annual Perseid meteor shower peaked on the day of a new moon — and a solar eclipse — so moonlight stayed out of the way. And there's more to look forward to: in December, the Geminids, the year's most prolific shower, will peak after a waxing crescent moon sets early in the evening, opening the door to excellent viewing. Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22. So, when and where can you catch the show?
